description: Turn your data scripts into fully functional, interactive web applications in minutes. Learn to use Dash (for enterprise) and Streamlit (for rapid prototyping).

slides.title: The Data App Problem
slides.content:
# Sharing Data 📤

You've written a beautiful Pandas script that analyzes sales data and generates Plotly charts. How do you share it with your boss?

You could send a static PDF, but they want to click drop-downs to filter by region.

You *could* spend 3 weeks building a React.js frontend and a FastAPI backend, but you are a Data Scientist, not a Full-Stack Web Developer.

This is where **Data App Frameworks** come in. They allow you to build full web apps using *only* Python.

slides.title: Introduction to Streamlit
slides.content:
# Rapid Prototyping: Streamlit 🎈

Streamlit is arguably the fastest way to build a data app. 

Its paradigm is incredibly simple: **The entire Python script reruns from top to bottom every time the user interacts with a widget on the screen.**

```bash
pip install streamlit
```

To run a Streamlit app, you don't run `python app.py`. You run:
```bash
streamlit run app.py
```

slides.title: Writing a Streamlit App
slides.content:
# The Streamlit Magic ✨

Streamlit widgets return values directly into your script. It is synchronous and straightforward.

```python_not
# app.py
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

st.title("My First Streamlit App")

# Create a slider widget. Its value is assigned to 'num_points'
num_points = st.slider("Number of points", min_value=10, max_value=1000)

# Generate random data based on the slider!
data = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(num_points, 2), columns=['x', 'y'])

# Display the data as a chart
st.scatter_chart(data)
```

When the user moves the slider to 500, the script instantly restarts, reads `num_points=500`, generates new data, and updates the chart!

slides.title: Streamlit Session State
slides.content:
# Preserving Data 💾

Because the script reruns entirely on every click, normal variables are destroyed and recreated.

If you want to remember something across reruns (like a score, or whether a user clicked a button previously), you must use `st.session_state`.

```python_not
import streamlit as st

# Initialize the state variable if it doesn't exist
if 'counter' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.counter = 0

# Create a button. If clicked, increment the state
if st.button("Click Me!"):
    st.session_state.counter += 1

# Display the state. It will survive reruns!
st.write(f"You clicked the button {st.session_state.counter} times.")
```

slides.title: Streamlit Caching
slides.content:
# Speeding it Up: `@st.cache_data` ⚡

If your script reruns every time a user clicks a dropdown, what happens if your script also downloads a 500MB CSV file from S3?

The app will freeze for 10 seconds on every click!

To prevent this, you decorate slow data-loading functions with `@st.cache_data`.

```python_not
import streamlit as st
import time

@st.cache_data
def load_massive_data():
    # Streamlit runs this ONCE, and stores the result in RAM.
    # On subsequent reruns, it skips this function entirely and returns the cached RAM data!
    time.sleep(5) # Simulate slow network
    return ["Data1", "Data2", "Data3"]

# This is instant after the first run!
data = load_massive_data()
st.write(data)
```

slides.title: Streamlit Quiz
slides.content: Check your understanding of Streamlit's architecture.
slides.quizQuestion: In Streamlit, what happens behind the scenes when a user interacts with a widget (like moving a slider)?
quizOptions: Streamlit makes an asynchronous AJAX call to a specific callback function.
Streamlit reruns the entire Python script from top to bottom, updating the variables with the new widget values.
Streamlit sends the widget value to a separate Node.js server.
Streamlit throws an error unless you define an `@st.callback`.

slides.title: Introduction to Dash
slides.content:
# Enterprise Apps: Dash 🏢

Streamlit is great, but its top-to-bottom rerun model struggles with massive, highly complex, multi-page enterprise applications.

**Dash** (created by the Plotly team) is the enterprise standard. It works entirely differently. 

Instead of rerunning the script, you define the UI Layout once, and then write specific `@callback` functions that tell Dash exactly which parts of the UI to update when a specific widget changes.

slides.title: The Dash Layout
slides.content:
# HTML in Python 🧱

In Dash, you build the DOM tree using Python classes that represent HTML tags (`html.Div`, `html.H1`) and Dash Core Components (`dcc.Graph`, `dcc.Slider`).

```python_not
from dash import Dash, html, dcc

app = Dash(__name__)

# Define the UI once
app.layout = html.Div([
    html.H1("My Dash Dashboard"),
    
    dcc.Dropdown(
        id='city-dropdown',
        options=[{'label': 'New York', 'value': 'NYC'}, {'label': 'London', 'value': 'LDN'}],
        value='NYC'
    ),
    
    # An empty container where the graph will go
    dcc.Graph(id='my-graph')
])

if __name__ == '__main__':
    app.run_server(debug=True)
```

slides.title: Dash Callbacks
slides.content:
# Reactive Updates: `@callback` ⚡

To make the dropdown update the graph, we define a callback. We tell Dash: *"Take the 'value' property of the 'city-dropdown', run this Python function, and output the result to the 'figure' property of the 'my-graph' component."*

```python_not
from dash import Input, Output, callback
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd

# ... (app.layout code from previous slide) ...

@callback(
    Output(component_id='my-graph', component_property='figure'),
    Input(component_id='city-dropdown', component_property='value')
)
def update_graph(selected_city):
    # This function ONLY runs when the dropdown changes!
    
    # (Normally you would filter a DataFrame based on selected_city here)
    df = pd.DataFrame({'Year': [2020, 2021], 'Sales': [100, 200]})
    
    # Generate a Plotly figure
    fig = px.bar(df, x="Year", y="Sales", title=f"Sales in {selected_city}")
    
    # Return the figure to the Output component
    return fig
```

slides.title: Dash DataTables
slides.content:
# Interactive Grids 📊

Dash includes incredibly powerful components for displaying tabular data. The `dash_table.DataTable` allows users to sort, filter, and edit data directly in the browser.

```python_not
from dash import dash_table
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plotly/datasets/master/solar.csv')

app.layout = html.Div([
    dash_table.DataTable(
        data=df.to_dict('records'),
        columns=[{"name": i, "id": i} for i in df.columns],
        filter_action="native", # Adds search bars to columns
        sort_action="native",   # Allows sorting
        page_size=10            # Adds pagination
    )
])
```

slides.title: Dash Quiz
slides.content: Test your knowledge of the Dash framework.
slides.quizQuestion: In Dash, what is the purpose of the `@callback` decorator?
quizOptions: It authenticates the user before they can view the dashboard.
It defines the HTML layout of the application.
It links the Input of a UI component (like a dropdown's value) to a Python function, and maps the function's return value to the Output of another component (like a graph).
It automatically downloads data from an SQL database.

slides.title: Summary
slides.content:
# Web App Developer! 🎉

You've learned how to turn scripts into scalable web applications.

## Key Takeaways

- ✅ **Data Apps:** Build frontends using only Python. No Javascript required.
- ✅ **Streamlit:** Ideal for rapid prototyping. The entire script reruns top-to-bottom on every interaction.
- ✅ **Streamlit State:** Use `@st.cache_data` to prevent slow data reloading, and `st.session_state` to remember variables across reruns.
- ✅ **Dash:** Ideal for complex, enterprise-grade applications. It uses an HTML-like layout tree and asynchronous callbacks.
- ✅ **Dash Callbacks:** Use `Input` and `Output` decorators to surgically update specific UI elements without reloading the whole page.
